criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and population access to piped drinking-water services (intradomiciliary and yard pipework coverage vs. unpiped sources) in urban and rural areas of Panama and Costa Rica.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: the paper does not examine any rule-type legal, administrative or regulatory mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules governing access, discretion/accommodation, enforcement/disconnection or utility ownership/regulatory rules governing connection). Instead, its regulatory references (Reglamento Técnico DGNTI-COPANIT 23-395-99 and Decreto Ejecutivo N°353 in Panama; Decreto Ejecutivo 38924-S and PNMSCSAP Decreto Ejecutivo N°33953-S-MINAET in Costa Rica; jurisdiction of ASEP, DISAPAS and ARESEP) concern technical drinking-water quality monitoring standards and potability surveillance among existing aqueducts (explaining why rural water quality is unrecorded in Panama), while remarks on weak/fragmented sector stewardship ('rectoría'), proposed 2017-2030 national policies and a recommendation to update tariffs in Panama are unanalysed macro-governance background and policy proposals. Under the plain literal wording of Criterion 2, the paper touches on institutional operator categories (IDAAN, JAARs, AyA, municipalities, ESPH, ASADAS), regulatory scope and national sector policies, which might superficially appear governance-related, but even under the plain reading it does not empirically examine a governance factor as an exposure determining service access (instead comparing national water coverage with public-health and GDP indicators), so plain_criterion2_decision is also exclude.
criterion_notes.c3: Compiles descriptive quantitative secondary statistics from national censuses/household surveys (INEC ENAHO July 2016 in Costa Rica; 2010 Census in Panama), regulatory records (ASEP, DISAPAS), national water laboratory surveillance (LNA across 2,588 aqueducts and 5,312 sources) and PAHO/WHO health/socioeconomic indicators, synthesised via PAHO consultancy visits and annual laboratory reporting. However, it is purely descriptive/ecological and lacks an empirical analytical design testing a governance mechanism on service access.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports population and household piped drinking-water coverage (94.6% piped coverage in Panama and 97.6% in Costa Rica in 2016; occupied dwellings with pipe inside dwelling, pipe outside dwelling or no pipe in Costa Rica in Cuadro 4), alongside potable water quality coverage (74.6% vs. 91.8%) and macro public-health indicators.
criterion_notes.c5: While national populations, occupied dwellings, operator categories and descriptive coverage/potability figures are reported, no legal or administrative exposure governing service access is operationalised or linked to an access outcome in an identifiable empirical design (drinking-water coverage is instead compared across the two countries as a correlate of public-health and socioeconomic indicators and 2030 SDG targets).
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in Spanish with an English title and abstract; translation/comprehension from the provided full text is straightforward and feasible under Criterion 10 (assessed directly from the Spanish full text by the AI screener).

study_design: Descriptive cross-national comparative study / sector situational diagnosis compiling secondary official statistics, household survey data and laboratory surveillance reports
country: Panama and Costa Rica (with Central American regional comparison in health/socioeconomic tables: Belize, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua and Panama)
population_and_sample: National populations and occupied dwellings in Panama (approx. 4,058,372 inhabitants; 130 urban and 5,619 rural aqueducts) and Costa Rica (4,889,762 inhabitants; 1,465,259 occupied dwellings in July 2016 ENAHO; 2,588 aqueducts and 5,312 water sources); unit of analysis: country, planning region/urban-rural zone and operator category
exposure: No rule-type legal, administrative or regulatory exposure governing service access analysed (descriptive comparison of national coverage/potability across countries and operator categories, technical water-quality monitoring regulations and macro health/socioeconomic indicators)
outcome: Piped drinking-water coverage (% population with piped water; occupied dwellings with indoor pipe, outdoor pipe or no pipe), potable drinking-water quality coverage (% receiving potable water) and national health indicators (life expectancy, under-5 mortality, communicable disease rate)
rationale: Excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure). Although the paper reports descriptive secondary statistics on household/population piped drinking-water coverage and water potability in Panama and Costa Rica (satisfying c1 and c4), it does not examine a rule-type legal, administrative, institutional or regulatory mechanism directly governing service access under Criterion 2. Instead, it presents a descriptive cross-national situational diagnosis comparing national water coverage with macro public-health and socioeconomic indicators (life expectancy, under-5 mortality, communicable diseases, literacy, GDP per capita, health expenditure) and 2022/2030 SDG policy targets. References to decrees and regulators (Reglamento Técnico DGNTI-COPANIT 23-395-99, Decreto Ejecutivo 38924-S, PNMSCSAP, ASEP, DISAPAS, ARESEP) concern technical water-quality potability standards and surveillance scope rather than rules governing household access or connection, and discussions of fragmented sector stewardship ('rectoría') and proposed 2030 national policies are unanalysed macro-governance background and policy recommendations. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, no governance exposure is empirically linked to a service-access outcome.
